Items.Authors: Adrianah E. Appleman
Items.Title: Calibration of CdTe Double-sided Strip Detectors for the SuperHERO Balloon-borne Hard X-ray Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Super – High Energy Replicated Optics (SuperHERO) balloon-borne telescope is designed to observe in the hard X-ray bandpass with unprecedented angular resolution. Scheduled for a two-day flight in 2028, SuperHERO will use MSFC’s replicated NiCo shell optics to achieve a technical goal of an angular resolution of a 10 arcseconds Half-Power Diameter (HPD) or better. Each of SuperHERO’s seven optical assemblies focuses onto a CdTe Double-sided Strip Detector (CdTe-DSD). Manufactured by iMAGINEX Inc., the CdTe-DSD design is based on the detectors used in the Hard X-ray Imager (HXI) on the Hitomi/Astro-H mission. Each detector consists of a 1 mm-thick, 34 × 34 mm² block of CdTe, encased between 128 orthogonal cathode and anode strips. The strips are 200 micron wide with a 250 micron pitch, well-matched to SuperHERO’s resolving power. Calibration of all CdTe-DSDs (seven flight units and one spare) was done at MSFC to determine gain, relative quantum efficiency, and spatial resolution.

Items.Authors: Yifan Zhang, Zijian Zhao, Yuxuan Zhu, Yusa Wang, Xiongtao Yang, Can Chen
Items.Title: Calibration of effective area for X-ray focusing mirrors with continuum from the perspective of simulation
Items.Abstract: Currently, driven by the demand for observational sensitivity, the combination of multiple focusing mirror modules is commonly adopted to enhance the effective area of telescope systems. This generates new requirements for ground - based calibration. To address this, we attempt to use detectors operating at high flux, such as SDDs, for the calibration of the effective area of focusing mirrors. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of the detector's energy spectral response on measurements through simulations, and based on these simulation results, we conduct research on corresponding correction methods.

Items.Authors: Ruixuan Matt Xie, Adrian K. Sinclair, James Burgoyne, Anthony I. Huber, Scott Chapman
Items.Title: CCAT: a two-octave 1.024 GHz KID readout featuring an overlap-channel polyphase synthesis filter bank on RFSoC
Items.Abstract: Next-generation submillimeter instruments require gigahertz-scale readout bandwidths to support the growing detector counts of large microwave kinetic inductance detector (KID) arrays. For the 850 GHz module of the Prime-Cam instrument on the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope, we have developed a KID readout system on an RFSoC with 1.024 GHz of instantaneous bandwidth, based on a parallelized overlap-channel polyphase synthesis filter bank and a matching receiving channelizer. The polyphase synthesis not only doubles the baseline readout channel count and bandwidth but also enables on-the-fly control of individual tone frequency, amplitude, and phase, facilitating optimized KID biasing. This capability is a gateway to tone tracking. We report key performance metrics, resource utilization, and scalability. Our results underscore the significance of advanced digital signal processing in furthering the state of the art in KID readout and enhancing submillimeter observations.

Items.Authors: Stephen C. Parshley, Ronan Higgins
Items.Title: CCAT: final assembly of the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST)
Items.Abstract: The Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST) is a 6-meter diameter, clear aperture, submillimeter (submm) / terahertz (THz) telescope for the CCAT Observatory. The crossed-Dragone optics are modified to correct for coma, resulting in a 7.8° field of view across a roughly 2-meter diameter focal plane. The primary and secondary mirrors are of comparable size and are composed of aluminum panels set on a carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer backup structure. The completed mirrors are mounted inside an Invar tipping structure, which is supported by a steel yoke. The system will deliver a total wavefront error of less than 22 microns at the focal plane. The observatory is located at an exquisite site for submm astronomy at 5600 meters above sea level on Cerro Chajnantor in the Atacama Desert. We present the transport and final assembly of FYST in Chile.

Items.Authors: James Burgoyne, Jason Austermann, Scott Chapman, Anthony I. Huber, Anna Vaskuri, Jordan Wheeler, Ruixan (Matt) Xie
Items.Title: CCAT: lithographic correction of an 850 GHz TiN MKID array
Items.Abstract: Prime-Cam, one of the first-light instruments for the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope developed by the CCAT Collaboration, will accommodate seven modules, including a central 850 GHz camera. The 850 GHz module uses three arrays of TiN microwave kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) totaling roughly 38,000 detectors, read out through 12 RF feedlines per array. As part of the characterization pipeline, we perform LED mapping to relate each detector’s measured resonant frequency to its physical position on the wafer. This enables a lithographic trimming step of the KID capacitors that significantly reduces frequency collisions and boosts usable detector yield. We present the design and laboratory characterization of one of the 850 GHz TiN arrays, with emphasis on the implementation, performance, and accuracy of the LED-based mapping procedure.

Items.Authors: Tilak Patel, CCAT Collaboration
Items.Title: CCAT: optimisation of the optical design of the 410 GHz module for Prime-Cam
Items.Abstract: Prime-Cam is a first-generation instrument for the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST), enabling wide-field, multi-frequency observations for cosmology, line-intensity mapping, and dust-rich galaxy studies. We present the optical design for the 410 GHz broadband module, which will deploy ~21,000 polarization-sensitive KID detectors to open a unique submillimeter window for Prime-Cam. Using Zemax OpticStudio, we evaluate system-length configurations, image-plane field curvature, and the trade-offs between Strehl ratio, FOV, and detector coupling. We also assess performance across the six outer module positions, where the crossed-Dragone telescope introduces varying aberrations. The design achieves high optical performance over the 1.3° FOV while remaining compatible with mechanical and manufacturing constraints.

Items.Authors: Christopher Mann, Kaitlyn Hessel, William Thompson, Christian Marois, Adam Johnson, Olivier Lardière, Joeleff Fitzsimmons, Sebastien Fabbro, Andre Fogal
Items.Title: CDI on SPIDERS: speckle removal post-processing techniques working towards 10^10 contrast
Items.Abstract: The SPIDERS instrument was designed to trailblaze new techniques and technologies for the next generation of high-contrast imaging instruments. First used as a laboratory test bench to experiment with and fine-tune our operational setup, SPIDERS has recently achieved an on-sky observing run at the Subaru telescope. Using laboratory calibration sources and real astronomical targets, we have benchmarked the improvement in imaging contrast achievable by this system via hardware and software means. Here we will specifically discuss the great strides and implementation techniques we have made with the Coherent Differential Imaging process, as well as the limitations we have encountered.

Items.Authors: Deborah C. Malone, Helawae F. Kelemu, Nazim A. Bharmal, Ronald Holzlöhner, Timothy Butterley, Angel Otarola, Miska Le Louarn, James Osborn, Tim J. Morris
Items.Title: Characterisation and modelling of dome turbulence through temporal covariances: CANARY and VLT analysis
Items.Abstract: This study develops methods for characterising dome turbulence using temporal covariances from open-loop on-sky data collected by the CANARY instrument on the William Herschel Telescope, as well as from detailed simulations of the telescope. These methods are then applied to pseudo open-loop telemetry from the VLT Adaptive Optics Facility to assess generalisation across instruments. Results show the importance of incorporating dome turbulence into adaptive optics simulations for accurate performance prediction.

Items.Authors: Philippa Downton, Thomas Buggey, Jesper Skottfelt, Douglas Jordan, David Hall
Items.Title: Characterisation of radiation induced defects in EM-CCDs for the Roman Space Telescope.
Items.Abstract: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope (RST) will be the first major mission to fly Electron-Multiplying Charge Coupled Devices (EM-CCDs) in the space environment. Operating at the L2 Lagrange point, RST will be exposed to high-energy particles capable of causing defects in the silicon lattice of an EM-CCD, potentially obscuring small signals. To characterise and help mitigate these radiation-induced defects, the trap pumping technique can be used. Trap pumping is a clocking method that enables the identification and analysis of individual charge traps, allowing sub-pixel locations, emission time constants, and densities of defects to be established. This paper presents the trap pumping methodology and experimental results obtained from a Teledyne-e2v CCD301. Measurements were performed at higher temperatures compared to previous literature to explore longer emission time traps. The experimental framework developed here will be applied to the CCD311, the modified flight detector for RST.

Items.Authors: Félix Sauvourel, Faustine Cantalloube, Philippe Delorme, Stephane Bergeon, Fabien Malbet
Items.Title: Characterisation of the wind-driven halo in high-contrast images: occurrence rate from 10 years of VLT/SPHERE-IRDIS data
Items.Abstract: Adaptive optics enables high-contrast imaging, but its temporal limitation, namely the servolag error, produces the so-called wind-driven halo (WDH) in the images. The WDH appears in the image as a low-spatial-frequency structure, whose morphology and intensity are governed primarily by high-altitude winds, in particular the jet stream flowing above Paranal. This WDH induces a contrast loss of up to one order of magnitude in the AO corrected-region. Using a new geometrical proxy, we analyse ten years of VLT/SPHERE high-contrast images and measure a WDH occurrence rate of about 70%, far exceeding previous estimates. This result shows that the servolag-induced aberrations in the focal plane image constitute an important limitation in current observations, and requires dedicated mitigation strategies for future high-contrast facilities.

Items.Authors: Ana Carolina Keiman Freire, Alejandro Farah Simon, Valente Vázquez-Velázquez, Rubén A. Flores-Meza, Fernando Ángeles , Joel Sánchez-Bermudez
Items.Title: Characterization and cryogenic validation of a mount for securing the new Ge grism for GRAVITY+ SUPER HIGH-RES mode
Items.Abstract: The GRAVITY+ project seeks to enhance the VLTI by boosting sensitivity and sky coverage, enabling K-band interferometry down to K≈22 mag and astrometric precision of ~20 μas. IA-UNAM and UCD are developing the new SUPER HIGH-RES mode (R≈15,000), which requires a redesigned filter wheel holding a germanium grism created by IA-UNAM and manufactured by Zeiss. This work reports the validation of the new cryogenic grism mount through tests of mounts made from PEEK, 5052-Al, 5083-Al, and 6061-Al. Mechanical stability under cryogenic conditions was evaluated using the COLIBRI cryostat, developed at IA-UNAM for advanced astronomical instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Jeronimo Calderon Gomez, Frantz Martinache, Nick Cvetojevic, Marc-Antoine Martinod, Vincent Foriel, Nemanja Jovanovic, Pradip Gatkine, David Mary, Roxanne Ligi, Sylvie Robbe-Dubois, Alexis Carlotti, Marc Ferlet, Matteo Pasinetti, Angelie Alagao, Arnaud Striffling, Guillermo Martin
Items.Title: Characterization and on-sky testing of photonic, AWG-based astronomical spectrographs
Items.Abstract: Astrophotonics intends to meet the needs of next-generation instruments at a small footprint, low cost, and high stability, compared to bulk-optics-based alternatives. Much development effort is driven by the stringent requirements of direct detection and characterisation of exoplanets.   Our team works in characterising Arrayed-Waveguide Grating (AWG) chips for photonics-based, high-resolution, near infrared spectroscopy. AWG spectrographs allow to test the feasibility of photonic spectro-interferometers for exoplanet characterization, another step towards fully photonic instruments for astronomy.  We present the current status of our AWG characterisation and a preliminary on-sky qualification campaign at the PAPYRUS AO system. We present the optical bench used, the spectrographs built for on-sky testing, and preliminary results using our high-resolution (H band) AWGs for a set of bright stars, assessing the capabilities of photonic spectroscopy for future compact instruments.

Items.Authors: Benjamin N. Hauptmann, Javier Rico, Giulio Lucchetta, Keerthana R. Lathika, Chiara Perrina, Philipp Azzarello, Juan Boix, David Gascón, Kimberly Keyser
Items.Title: Characterization of the BETA64 read-out-system for the FIT instrument
Items.Abstract: The scintillating Fiber Tracker (FIT) is a tracking detector for space applications, composed of mats of plastic scintillator fibers and read out by custom silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays. FIT can reconstruct the charge and direction of ionizing particles and enhance the angular resolution of gamma-ray detectors in the MeV to GeV regime.    A custom, low-power ( 5 for single photoelectrons enables charge measurement from Hydrogen to Iron. After characterization of the 16-channel prototype, the 64-channel BETA64 has been completed, characterized, and integrated into a FIT prototype, enabling the measurement of ion tracks. This contribution presents the preliminary results of the BETA64 characterization and the FIT performance in terms of spatial resolution, particle identification and trigger efficiency.

Items.Authors: Enrico Congiu, Fuyan Bian, Carlo Felice Manara, Arseniy Kuznetsov, Guido Agapito, Lisa-Marie Mazzolo, Benoît Neichel, Cédric Plantet, Fabio Rossi, Fernando Selman
Items.Title: Characterization of the MUSE NFM PSF as a function of atmospheric conditions
Items.Abstract: The Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) achieves exceptional spatial resolution in narrow-field mode (NFM) thanks to its GALACSI adaptive optics (AO) system, yet limitations in point spread function (PSF) characterization still hinder full exploitation of its capabilities. We analyzed a large set of historical standard-star observations to quantify how NFM PSF properties vary with observing conditions, including elevation, seeing, coherence time, wind speed, and wavelength. These empirical relations were used to calibrate TipTop, a fast AO-PSF simulation tool soon to be integrated into the ESO Exposure Time Calculator. Our results confirm that calibration with real on-sky data is essential for accurate PSF modeling. Once implemented, this will provide condition-specific NFM PSF predictions and more reliable signal-to-noise estimates. In the longer term, TipTop may also enable PSF reconstruction for individual observations, significantly improving data analysis and quality control.

Items.Authors: Charles-Antoine Claveau, Trevor T. Nguyen, Hannah Gulick, Jessica R. Lu, Steven V. W. Beckwith, Kodi Rider
Items.Title: Characterization of the Sony Pregius S IMX530 CMOS detector for high-bandwidth AO and wide-field survey applications
Items.Abstract: Low-cost, high-performance CMOS detectors enable astronomical instruments with many focal-plane channels. Multi-conjugate adaptive optics uses multiple Shack–Hartmann wave-front sensors at high frame rates with sub-pixel centroiding, while space-based and wide-field survey imagers require large-format, small-pixel detectors with low dark current for long integrations; in all cases, low read noise is critical. We present a laboratory characterization of the Sony Pregius S IMX530 CMOS sensor integrated into the QHY530ProII camera. At 10 °C we measure a median dark current of 8.8 e⁻ px⁻¹ ks⁻¹, readout noise of 1.7 e⁻ rms, temporal signal stability of 0.05% peak-to-peak, ≃0.8% non-linearity, inter-pixel capacitance <0.1%, and read-noise correlations ≃0.5%. Astrometric tests yield centroiding precision of 0.012 pixel with systematic errors <0.01 pixel. We also report frame rates and windowed high-speed operation for high-bandwidth wave-front sensing.

Items.Authors: Moses K. Mogotsi
Items.Title: Characterizing the performance and long term stability of a degraded H2RG detector
Items.Abstract: NIRWALS is a near-infrared integral field spectrograph on the Southern African Large Telescope (SALT) that utilizes a Hawaii-2RG detector and extends the wavelength coverage of SALT to 0.8–1.7 microns. The detector degraded over time while in storage, resulting in an estimated 11% of the detector pixels becoming unusable for science observations. We have studied the stability and performance of the detector over the past two years to determine how the degradation has affected it and to more precisely identify which pixels are least reliable for operations.

Items.Authors: Seery Chen
Items.Title: CMOS Detector Characterization for the MOTHRA 1140-Lens Array
Items.Abstract: MOTHRA is an array of 1,140 telephoto lenses, each equipped with ultra-narrow bandpass filters and CMOS cameras, and will be equivalent to a 4.7 m f/0.08 refractor when complete. Based on the design of the Dragonfly Spectral Line Mapper, major hardware upgrades have been implemented, resulting in a line mapping sensitivity that will be an order of magnitude deeper than any other facility. As part of this upgrade, we take advantage of recent improvements in CMOS detector technology, and use cameras with Sony IMX571 and IMX445 detectors. Here, we evaluate the read noise, fixed pattern noise, dark current, bias stability, quantum efficiency, and performance at varying gain settings. We compare these measurements with the performance of past cameras used on the Dragonfly arrays, and present preliminary SBContrast surface-brightness limit estimates calculated from early commissioning data. These measurements will inform calibration and observational strategies for the new telephoto array.

Items.Authors: Airam Salas, Maria Begoña García-Lorenzo, Julio Castro-Almazán
Items.Title: CNN-based reanalysis of optical turbulence at the Canary Islands Observatories
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric optical turbulence degrades ground-based observations, and its vertical distribution, given by Cn₂(h), determines key site parameters for high spatial resolution astronomy. The Canary Islands Observatories (OCAN) obtained over 200 nights of Generalized SCIDAR profiles, forming a large turbulence database. We present a CNN-based reanalysis of this dataset, supported by an end-to-end ETL pipeline for efficient preprocessing, mapping and tensor generation. Turbulence maps are converted into multi-channel tensors and processed through pre-trained CNNs used as frozen feature extractors to obtain deep embeddings. Unsupervised clustering of these embeddings reveals latent atmospheric regimes. This approach offers new insights into turbulence variability at OCAN and showcases a novel large-scale characterization method using modern deep-learning techniques.

Items.Authors: Thomas Benedict, Marc Baril, Gregory Barrick
Items.Title: Coating mirrors at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, twenty years of lessons learned
Items.Abstract: The Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope Corporation maintains a 4m filament-based mirror coating facility that has been in service since before first light in 1979. In addition to the CFHT M1 and M2 mirrors, it also serves as the coating facility for several other observatories located in Hawaii, including the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope (UKIRT), the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF), and the Faulkes Telescope North, located on the summit of Haleakala on Maui. Though some changes to the coating process took place during the years from 1979 until 2000, a series of investigations between 2005 and present day led to a number of changes in the stripping, cleaning, and coating procedure. This paper explores the lessons learned, the changes that were made, and presents the current state of the coating process at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope.

Items.Authors: Laurent M. Mugnier, Alice Fontbonne, Pauline Trouvé, Olivier Herscovici-Schiller, Frédéric Champagnat, Yann Lucas, Yann Lai-Tim, Frédéric Cassaing
Items.Title: Co-design approach to aperture masking
Items.Abstract: Aperture masking interferometry is a technique originally designed to alleviate the influence of atmospheric turbulence on images recorded on ground-based telescopes.   In this communication we explore the optimization of the aperture mask by an optical/digital co-design approach in order to obtain diffraction-limited images of relatively bright objects imaged through turbulence.  We show that, with a few simplifying assumptions, it is possible to express the Mean Square Error of the restored image as a function of the chosen mask, of the spatial Power Spectral Density (PSD) of the observed object and of the noise level, without actually computing any image.   This allows us to optimize the aperture mask with a reduced computing cost.  We also implement a multi-frame blind deconvolution algorithm to estimate jointly the observed object and the piston in front of each subaperture, and check by simulations that the aperture masks obtained indeed allow a satisfactory image reconstruction.

Items.Authors: Marta Maria Civitani, Stefano Basso, Riccardo Belmonte, Massimiliano Cariraghi, Vincenzo Cotroneo, Mauro Ghigo, Edoardo Redaelli, Daniele Spiga, Gabriele Vecchi, Luigi Lessio, Salvatore Incorvaia, Luca Schettini, Giorgio Toso
Items.Title: Cold glass slumping optics for the custom hybrid X-ray telescope of the International Axion Observatory (IAXO)
Items.Abstract: Thin-glass technology enables the production of ultra-thin foils that can be cold-bent to very small radii without fracture, while maintaining excellent micro-roughness. These features make them well suited for rapid, cost-effective cold-replication of grazing-incidence X-ray optics. The CGSO process, patented by INAF-OABrera, shapes flat glass foils on precision mandrels and bonds them onto a support structure using Wolter-I counter-form moulds and reinforcing ribs that ensure structural integrity and suppress low-frequency shape errors. This work extends and validates the process for shorter, 5 m focal-length optics required for the BabyIAXO hybrid design, which features an inner core and an outer corona to cover the 700mm magnetic bore. The reduced focal length requires a full redesign of the integration machine to handle higher mandrel curvature and larger angular adjustments. We present the project, the upgraded strategy, expected performance.

Items.Authors: Daniel Bednarski, Carlos E. Fermino, Karim Kaismoune, Alan Uomoto, Jeffrey D. Crane, Solange Ramírez, Rafael A. Ribeiro
Items.Title: ComCam preliminary software design – a systemic approach
Items.Abstract: ComCam is a medium-field visible imager conceived as a test camera – and likely a science instrument – for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). In terms of operation, the ComCam Device Control System (DCS) is responsible for all internal functionalities, responding to the Observatory Control System (OCS) at the top level, which orchestrates each DCS among ~30 controllable subsystems. The GMT adopts a domain engineering approach, in which a metamodel describes the observatory-wide architecture and a software development kit (SDK) is provided for DCS implementation.    This work presents the systemic approach employed in developing the ComCam software design, suited to the compliance with GMT standards. A SysML model was developed using Visual Paradigm tool to capture the products from analysis to design, and to establish a partial representation of the ComCam DCS. Finally, the software components (e.g., controllers) and their properties could be transcribed into SDK specification files.

Items.Authors: Danielle N. Gurgew
Items.Title: Commissioning of a custom dual linear magnetron system for the development of high-energy multilayer coatings for full-shell X-ray optics
Items.Abstract: A custom dual-linear magnetron assembly is undergoing commissioning to enable direct deposition of complex reflective coatings for full-shell X-ray optics at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC). Designed to achieve +/- 2% non-uniformity along the nominal 600 mm shell lengths, these 32 in x 1.5 in magnetrons are mounted back-to-back with 180 degree separation, allowing for layer-by-layer deposition within a closed geometry. Shells with diameters ranging from ~190 mm to ~1.5 m can be accommodated. Custom collimators and masking are also optimized and integrated into the system while plans for a shutter mechanism are in progress. This system dramatically increases MSFC’s end-to-end fabrication capabilities for high angular-resolution full-shell X-ray optics, particularly in the hard X-ray to soft gamma-ray bandpass. Initial results from the commissioning and optimization process for several current projects are presented along with a discussion on use for future mission concepts.

Items.Authors: George Heald, Shivani Bhandari, Giulia Macario, Sam Mcsweeney, Alec Thomson, Randall Wayth, Xiang Zhang, Betsey Adams, Ian Heywood
Items.Title: Commissioning SKA-Low: results and plans towards Science Verification
Items.Abstract: SKAO's SKA-Low will be the most sensitive radio telescope operating in the 50–350 MHz frequency range. Built in the remote Murchison region of Western Australia, it will ultimately comprise 512 stations, each with 256 dual-polarization antennas, distributed over a 74 km maximum baseline. The telescope has entered a pivotal commissioning phase. The first four-station Array Assembly 0.5 (AA0.5) has delivered successful early results, including system-stability tests, calibration development, beamforming, known pulsar detections, sensitivity validation, and initial interferometric imaging. We present an overview of SKA-Low Science Commissioning, highlighting results from AA0.5, early outcomes from AA1, and plans for upcoming phases, including scaling to longer baselines, advanced calibration, and increased operational robustness. These efforts lay the groundwork for the upcoming AA2 Science Verification phase, which will provide the community’s first access to SKA-Low science ready data.

Items.Authors: Risa Shimizu, Masayuki Hirabayashi, Bungo Ikenoue, Masaki Morita, Ryouhei Kano, Ko Hosokawa, Takehiko Wada, Kazuhisa Mitsuda, Chihiro Tokoku, Ichiro Mase, Fumihiko Usui, Hirokazu Kataza
Items.Title: Conceptual system design of the JASMINE Detector Box Unit and evaluation of its cooling components
Items.Abstract: JASMINE (Japan Astrometry Satellite Mission for INfrared Exploration) aims for ultra-high-precision infrared astrometry. Its onboard instrument requires stringent stability, and the infrared detectors must be maintained at 173 K within a 273 K enclosure. The Detector Box Unit (DBU), under conceptual design at the Advanced Technology Center of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, provides the cooling function to keep the infrared detectors at required temperature, using a vibration-free thermo-electric cooler (TEC) and a graphite thermal strap with high conductance connecting the DBU and a radiator. The radiator interface limits heat rejection to 12 W at 200 K, where the functionality of the TEC and thermal strap is not guaranteed. We are conducting device-level tests to evaluate their performance and incorporating the results into the DBU design. This presentation reports the design approach and findings from TEC and thermal strap characterization.

Items.Authors: Andres Pino Pavez
Items.Title: Continuous Integration of Operations and Data Quality: The TIO Model at ESO’s Paranal Observatory
Items.Abstract: As part of Paranal Observatory’s ongoing evolution toward more efficient and autonomous scientific operations, the Telescope and Instrument Operators (TIO) Group has played a key role in redefining how observations are executed and validated. This transformation has reshaped the operational model and strengthened the connection between technical expertise and scientific data quality.    The purpose of this talk is to present how the TIO Group at Paranal Observatory has evolved to meet the changing demands of scientific operations. It will describe the transition toward greater autonomy in nightly observing activities, the implementation of comprehensive training and certification programs, and the development of integrated processes that ensure scientific data quality. The talk will also highlight how these advancements are preparing the TIO team to operate the next-generation systems of the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT).

Items.Authors: Aaron M. Hunter, Philip Hinz, Gabriel Kruglikov
Items.Title: Control and electronics architecture for large adaptive secondary mirrors
Items.Abstract: (ASM) for the Keck 1 telescope. An ASM has advantages over an adaptive optic system at a telescope port, however, it also brings significant engineering challenges, primarily heat dissipation over the primary mirror.     This work discusses the electrical design and control system architecture for the ASM which . will have at least 2500 linear electromechanical actuators across its surface. We present results on three different control approaches, balancing the dynamic performance of an analog driver with the lower power requirements of a pulse-width modulated driver.     Another significant challenge in ASM control is the transmission of the control signals at rates dictated by wavefront sensors (>1KHz). We present three methods for parallelizing the control signals in order to meet this requirement.    Finally, we present the overview of the overall architecture and its interface to the Keck telescope.

Items.Authors: Piero D'Incecco, Mauro Dolci, Gianluca Di Rico, Aleksei Martynov, Gaetano Di Achille, Philippa J. Mason, Gerard Gallardo i Peres, James B. Garvin, Justin R. Filiberto, Elizabeth B. Rampe, Sriram S. Bhiravarasu, Tibor Kremic, Stefano Branca, Rosa Anna Corsaro, Carmelo Monaco, Iván López, Pier Raffaele Platania, Goro Komatsu, Dmitry Gorinov, Giuseppe Salerno, Edoardo Spezzati, Domenico Tescione, Alessandra Ciappa, Clive Oppenheimer, Stefano Di Frischia, Gaetano Valentini, Matteo Canzari
Items.Title: CONVERGE: a Venus lander–orbiter mission concept for in-situ geophysical and atmospheric measurements
Items.Abstract: CONVERGE (COordinated Network for Venus Exploration and Research with Ground Experiments) is a European mission concept that combines an orbiter, a short-lived lander, and a longer-lived passive seismic node to obtain new in-situ measurements from the surface of Venus. The mission targets a geologically young region such as Imdr Regio, one of the proposed “young volcanic rises,” to investigate recent interior activity, surface evolution, and atmosphere–surface interactions.    The lander would perform mineralogical (XRD/XRF) and elemental analyses, atmospheric profiling during descent, and passive seismic monitoring on the surface. Even with a limited lifetime, these measurements would provide critical ground truth for radar, spectroscopy, and atmospheric retrievals from missions such as DAVINCI, VERITAS, EnVision, Venera-D, and the Venus Orbiter Mission, and would inform models of rocky exoplanets observed by PLATO, ARIEL, and NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory.

Items.Authors: Simone Sacquegna, Benedetta Di Francesco, Gianluca Di Rico, Fernando Pedichini, Elisa Portaluri, Simone Antoniucci, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Maciej W. Bajor, Gianluca Li Causi, Roberto Piazzesi
Items.Title: Convolutional neural network for the PSF subtraction in high contrast imaging: a performance analysis
Items.Abstract: Thanks to Adaptive Optics systems, ground-based telescopes in the 8m class have been successful in detecting exoplanets through direct imaging, starting with the infrared bands, and recently also in the visible, with the Hα observations of PDS 70 b,c and WISPIT 2 b protoplanets.  One of the hardest parts of exoplanet detection is the data post-processing, in particular distinguishing the planet signal from the speckle noise of the parent star in which it is embedded (by reconstructing and removing the PSF of the star from the image); the planet is indeed often 10^5 or more times fainter than the star.  Typical algorithms such as ADI - PCA rely on the statistical analysis of the data sequence. In this work, we are proposing the use of a trained neural network as a robust estimator of the parent star PSF, using precise simulations of telescope observations in which the PSF is generated through a complete physical optics system, generating pairs of ideal and corrupted images of the field.

Items.Authors: Riccardo Falco, Andrea Bulgarelli, Nicolò Parmiggiani, Valentina Fioretti, Laura Di Gesu, Eric Burns, Luca Castaldini, Elisabetta Cavazzuti, Valerio D'Elia, Ambra Di Piano, Tori Fae, Antonio Femia, Francesco Fenu, Eliza Neights, Wing Ma, Mattia Maniscalco, Israel Martinez Castellanos, Ghulam Mustafa, Gabriele Panebianco, Alessandro Rizzo, Claudio Sartori, Yong Sheng, Fabrizio Tavecchio, Steven Boggs, Eric Wulf, Dieter Hartmann, Carolyn Kierans, John Tomsick, Andreas Zoglauer
Items.Title: COSIflow: a modular framework for orchestrating and monitoring automated scientific pipelines for the COSI mission
Items.Abstract: The Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) is a NASA mission that surveys the MeV gamma-ray sky through high-resolution spectroscopy, Compton imaging and polarisation measurements. To meet its science data processing needs and enable rapid follow-up of GRB detections, we developed COSIflow, a workflow framework extending Apache Airflow with mission-specific capabilities. Through its COSIDAG class, COSIflow standardises scientific pipeline construction and supports parallel, reproducible workflows. We present operational pipelines such as the Fast Transient Pipeline that analyse data downlinked via TDRSS after an onboard trigger, which will be based on COSIflow.

Items.Authors: Horst Steuer, Markus Feldt, Andreas Obereder, Stefan Raffetseder, Thomas Bertram, Carlos Correia, Hugo Coppejans, Martin Kulas, Silvia Scheithauer, Florian Briegel
Items.Title: Creating an ELT scale command matrix for METIS in less than one second on a consumer grade GPU using Python
Items.Abstract: METIS, the Mid-infrared ELT Imager and Spectrograph, one of the first instruments to be used at ESO’s 39m Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), will use its Single Conjugate Adaptive Optics (SCAO) system for all observing modes. An essential part of SCAO will be the command matrix which will be used to reconstruct wavefront information in the control space of the deformable mirror M4 of the ELT from measurements of the pyramid wavefront sensor on the hard real-time computer. Both, the pupil and M4, are not fixed with regard to the pyramid wavefront sensor, making an update of the command matrix every 2 seconds necessary in the worst case.  In this presentation we show that we are able to produce a command matrix on the fly in less than one second on consumer grade hardware using a single GPU by approaching the problem in an innovative way. In an end-to-end simulation we show that the approach does not compromise any accuracy and that M4 misregistration is being handled well.

Items.Authors: That Minh Bao Ton, Damien Prêle, Manuel Gonzalez, Jean Mesquida, Didier Charrier, Edouard Bechetoille
Items.Title: Cryogenic low Flicker noise amplifier optimized for superconducting detectors in X-Ray astronomy
Items.Abstract: Optimized for the Athena X-IFU, a cryogenic SiGe BiCMOS LNA addresses the critical challenge of flicker noise. By leveraging analytical models and geometric sizing, the design targets a noise floor below 1 nV/√Hz down to 1 Hz. Experimental results from a fabricated prototype confirm its suitability for superconducting detector applications.

Items.Authors: Olaf Iwert
Items.Title: Curved Imaging Detectors - New Possibilities in Optical System Design
Items.Abstract: The presence of Petzval field curvature in any optical system has so far mostly been dealt with purely from an optical design point of view: separating efforts by introducing optical field flatteners and producing electronic imaging detectors which are as flat as possible for fast imaging optics. Contrary to that - from a system point of view - it does make sense to consider detector and optical system not as isolated units, but to think “out-of-the-box” to overcome this problem with a curved detector and herewith to increase the system performance beyond current limitations of the conventional scheme. This paper is an overview of the optical motivation for curved detectors in different fields and describes the associated findings on different examples. It also tries to summarize some of the curved detector developments of the past years (since earlier papers of the author) with an outlook to future developments.

Items.Authors: Yoshiyuki Kubo
Items.Title: Data reduction pipeline for the PETREL CMOS sensor: row-correlated temporal read noise removal, synthetic darks, and non-uniform flat correction
Items.Abstract: PETREL is a microsatellite designed for wide-field near-UV observations of transients. This study focuses on the development of its ground-based reduction pipeline.  The CMOS sensor bias exhibits a temperature-dependent structure and row-correlated temporal noise. We proposed a method to extract and remove these components from the observed images themselves. Furthermore, addressing strict operational constraints in orbit where standard calibration is impossible, we synthesized dark frames by stacking sky images and created flat frames using onboard LEDs.  As a result, simulations applying this reduction estimated a limiting magnitude of 19.0 with an integration time of 1500 seconds. This sensitivity is sufficient to detect supernova shock breakouts out to100 Mpc within 0.1 days of their onset, confirming the mission's scientific feasibility.

Items.Authors: Isaac Bernardino Dinis, Nicolas Blind, Muskan Shinde, Bruno Chazelas, Nathanael Restori, Christophe Lovis, Sylvain Cetre, Angelie Alagao, Romain Fetick, Taïssir Heritier, Benoît Neichel, Thierry Fusco, Jean-François Sauvage, Vincent Chambouleyron
Items.Title: DD4AO control law for RISTRETTO: robustness, real-time performance, and on-sky validation with PAPYRUS
Items.Abstract: RISTRETTO is a VLT visitor instrument for characterizing nearby exoplanet atmospheres via high-contrast, high-resolution spectroscopy. Its key goal is detecting reflected light from planets such as Proxima Centauri b at ~35 mas (~2 λ/D at 750 nm), which demands an AO strategy that performs reliably at very small separations.  We apply DD4AO—an optimal, data-driven control law—to the RISTRETTO real-time control system. DD4AO convexifies the AO control problem to guarantee robustness and stability while preserving strong disturbance rejection. Because it is non-parametric and solved at discrete frequencies, it relies only on measured frequency responses of components and disturbances, with no need for analytical models.  We assess robustness, stability margins, latency, and real-time behavior in a realistic RTC setup. On-sky tests with PAPYRUS demonstrate stable closed-loop performance, showing that DD4AO is a practical, plug-and-play control solution for next-generation high-contrast AO.

Items.Authors: Xavier Coulon, Bruno Maffei, Nabila Aghanim
Items.Title: Decision-tree guided instrumental optimisation for CMB spectral distortion measurements with an FTS
Items.Abstract: The COBE/FIRAS mission showed that the CMB spectrum is extremely close to a perfect blackbody, although tiny departures known as spectral distortions are expected. The main signatures, the y-distortion and the mu-distortion, arise from energy release and provide unique information on the thermal history of the Universe that no other observable can access. I will present the latest optimisation study of FTS-based instruments dedicated to CMB spectral distortion measurements, such as the balloon-borne experiment BISOU (CNES Phase A) and the FOSSIL M-class mission submitted to the ESA M8 call. I used decision trees to explore the multidimensional space of instrumental and observational parameters and to quantify their impact on sensitivity to CMB spectral distortions and to the cosmic infrared background (CIB). These results highlight the most efficient instrument and observation optimisation strategies for designing future missions dedicated to CMB spectral distortions.

Items.Authors: Dirk Schmidt, Andrew Beard
Items.Title: Declustered: the KAOS Evo 2 DKIST MCAO real-time control system
Items.Abstract: Realtime control (RTC) for multi-conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) in the 4-meter Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) is one of the most computationally demanding tasks in astronomical AO today. Nine wavefront sensors (1k x 1k px each) and a total of ~12k cross-correlation subapertures (20 x 20 px each) must be analyzed and 3 deformable mirrors (~3.5k actuators) commanded at a rate of 2 kHz. Initially planned to use a 10-server cluster, we meanwhile accomplished to run the entire RTC in a single server with 192 AMD Zen 4 CPU cores. This is possible due to optimized programing and efficient use of these CPUs. We abandoned the cluster approach, greatly simplifying the hard- and software architecture, operational complexity and substantially saving electrical power by using only a single server.    We present the KAOS Evo 2 DKIST MCAO RTC architecture and discuss key programming techniques for efficient use of contemporary CPUs enabling fast, low-latency RTCs for very large AO systems.

Items.Authors: Alina Malow
Items.Title: Deep-learning-supported depth-from-focus-microscope
Items.Abstract: Compact sensor systems, such as those used in rover missions, can profit from 3D measurement techniques that are both accurate and resource-efficient. The Depth-from-Focus (DFF) method derives depth information solely from variations in focus and requires no additional hardware beyond a camera system. Compared to classic DFF-approaches Deep Depth-from-Focus (DDFF) methods using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can reduce the number of images needed for depth estimation. This lowers both energy consumption and memory requirements. In this work, a microscope setup was upgraded with a DDFF capability, demonstrating how DDFF can be applied to the measurement of geological samples. A beam splitter enables the microscope to operate in combination with a spectrometer. One potential application is to use depth information obtained via DDFF to provide contextual data for spectral measurements.

Items.Authors: Felipe Daruich
Items.Title: Defining a unified and modular electronics platform for NOIRLab observatories
Items.Abstract: NOIRLab’s telescopes rely on electronics and control systems built across different technological eras, creating a fragmented environment with high maintenance demands and growing obsolescence risks. The integration of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory demonstrates the advantages of modern, industrial-grade, standards-compliant technologies and provides a model for improving long-term maintainability and operational efficiency.  This paper proposes a strategic framework for developing a unified, modular electronics platform across NOIRLab facilities, emphasizing standardization, subsystem reusability, and industry-supported architectures—from servo controls and active optics to PLC-based interlocks and detector controllers. The goal is to initiate discussion and outline a path toward a sustainable, scalable, and resilient electronics ecosystem that enhances reliability and scientific productivity across NOIRLab observatories.

Items.Authors: Matthew Werneken, Danielle Frostig, Phillip Cargile, Vedant Chandra, Liam Connor, Charlie Conroy, Peter Doherty, Daniel Fabricant, Benjamin Johnson, Mark Mueller, John J. Piotrowski, V. Ashley Villar
Items.Title: Defining system requirements and science drivers for boombox, twin high-throughput spectrographs on 6.5m MMT and Magellan Telescopes
Items.Abstract: Boombox is a pair of high-throughput optical spectrographs being commissioned with the Via Survey in 2027 to provide dual-hemisphere, r=23.5 mag spectroscopy (R~1000; 355-1010 nm) of transients. With 36 fibers over 1 deg^2, high throughput, and 100 nights/yr observing time, Boombox is uniquely poised to capture the 24th-magnitude LSST sky in spectra. Boombox will drive 10% of the survey, enabling rapid follow-up to LSST and GW transients, precursor candidate studies, and statistical catalogs of faint targets across astronomy: rare transients, UV-bright SLSNe, halo stars, FRB hosts, and beyond. We present the driving system requirements for Boombox, based on the primary time-domain science and many secondary objectives. This includes science drivers and key deliverables, flowing into detailed system requirements, optical design, and hardware selections. We review instrument trade studies, inputs from the broader Via survey, and corresponding decisions made to maximize science output.

Items.Authors: Albert Ostoja-Starzewski, Thomas Hall, Elizabeth Keefe, Mason Black, Kerri Cahoy, Michael Shao, John Monnier, Leonid Pogorelyuk
Items.Title: Demonstration of an adjustable 1-5 meter five-mirror piezoelectric compact delay line for space interferometry
Items.Abstract: Precise optical path length (OPL) control is essential for formation-flying interferometer mission concepts, where independent spacecraft motion continuously perturbs the optical path between collectors. For dual-tracking architectures, in which the delay line rapidly switches between a reference star and a science target, we demonstrate a compact laboratory five-mirror delay-line system capable of continuous OPL measurement and control over several meters. We integrate a tunable laser, used in conjunction with a quadrature-channel interferometer, to directly measure and validate OPL with sub-100-micron accuracy. Our demonstration shows the elements needed for dual-tracking: a continuously adjustable 1-5 m delay line with sub-100-micron control, and reliable switching between the reference and science channels.

Items.Authors: Wilbert G. Ras-Vinke, Kevin Kouwenhoven, Jochem J. A. Baselmans, Kenichi Karatsu, David J. Thoen, Vignesh Murugesan, Pieter J. de Visser
Items.Title: Demonstration of Single Photon Counting With Kinetic Inductance Detectors From 4 to 25 μm
Items.Abstract: One of the major goals of modern astronomy is the atmospheric characterization of Earth-like exoplanets in the optical and infrared. Extremely sensitive detectors are required to measure the exoplanet’s faint signal down to the single-photon level with near-zero dark count rates. Especially in the mid-infrared - the target band for the Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE) mission concept - semiconducting technologies are unable to meet the requirements. Therefore, we demonstrate single-photon counting with superconducting, Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors at the wavelengths 3.8, 8.5, 18.5 and 25 μm and measure dark count rates of 3, 6, 20 and 22 mHz with resolving powers (E/δE) of 9.9, 6.0, 3.2, 3.3, respectively. These results demonstrate the MKID detector technology in the mid-infrared and the intricate measurement setups required. We discuss how the detector design and measurement setup can be further optimized to improve the detector performance in the mid-infrared.

Items.Authors: Dylan M. McKeithen
Items.Title: Deriving wavefront and pointing stability requirements for SHERA using a differentiable two-mirror dLux forward model
Items.Abstract: We present a differentiable Fresnel optical model to derive wavefront and pointing stability requirements for the proposed SHERA (Searching for Habitable Exoplanets with Relative Astrometry) SMEX mission, which will use a diffractive pupil for micro-arcsecond relative astrometry of nearby Sun-like binaries to search for rocky exoplanets. Implemented in the dLux framework, the model propagates between the primary pupil, an intermediate pupil at the secondary mirror, and the detector, capturing spatially varying wavefront error (WFE) and beamwalk across the secondary. We perform parameter inference in the eigenbasis of the Fisher information matrix for the joint parameter space to suppress degeneracies that drive astrometric bias. Simulated observing campaigns then map WFE and pointing jitter into astrometric precision, yielding nominal stability requirements consistent with SHERA’s performance goals.

Items.Authors: Tommaso Lapucci, Lorenzo Busoni, Alfio Puglisi, Marco Bonaglia, Stefan Ströbele, Nicholas Devaney
Items.Title: Design and implementation of a new PLC based control electronics for the NACO deformable mirror
Items.Abstract: We present a new control electronics architecture for the NACO deformable mirror (DM), developed for the MORFEO test unit. The system uses industrial PLC technology with EtherCAT terminals, the ESO-recommended standard. A Beckhoff CX2040 embedded PC manages real-time software, signal generation, and communication. The DM’s 185 analog channels (±10 V) are driven by 48 EL4134 terminals at ~1 kS/s. Deterministic communication with the adaptive optics RTC is achieved via an EL6601 Ethernet terminal receiving MUDPI packets containing DM shape vectors, which are applied through the high-voltage amplifiers. Analog performance such as resolution, noise, drift, and hysteresis have been tested to confirm the feasibility of the design. The modular architecture provides a versatile, cost-effective platform adaptable to DMs with different actuator counts and integrates seamlessly with the ESO control framework.

Items.Authors: Can Chen
Items.Title: Design and test of a time-varying X-ray source for eXTP-SFA X-ray telescope
Items.Abstract: In order to evaluate the timing performance of the Spectroscopy Focusing Array (SFA) telescopes, an time-varying X-ray source based on a grid pole-controlled X-ray tube was designed and integrated into in the 100-m X-ray Test Facility in China. This time-varying X-ray source can generate pulsed X-rays with short duration (e.g., 100 ns) or any X-ray light curve. In this report, we will present the design of the time-varying X-ray source and the test results of not only the SFA telescopes but also some already launched X-ray telescopes (GECAM, EP), including time resolution, time accuracy calibration (in Pulse mode), and time-varying response (in Light Curve mode).

Items.Authors: Annino Vaccarella, Lu Wang, Joice Mathew, Doris Grosse, Robert Sharp, Alexey Grigoriev, Gregory Jolley, Mark Downing, Michael Ellis, Marc White, Hana Benhizia, Nian Jiang, Warrick Schofield, Francis Bennet, Gaston Gausachs
Items.Title: Design and Testing of a Unified Packaging Solution for the Leonardo Saphira QM and Saphira Optitrax Detectors
Items.Abstract: The Leonardo Saphira 512×512 (“Large Saphira”) detector is available in two configurations: the Saphira QM for wavefront sensing and the Saphira OptiTrax for satellite optical communications. The OptiTrax variant includes a central region optimized for high-speed optical communication, which requires radio-frequency buffering and additional bias supplies not supported by the existing Saphira QM packaging. To address these requirements, the Australian National University (ANU) has developed a unified packaging solution compatible with both detector versions. The design integrates isolation capacitors and diode protection circuits on the underside of the package to mitigate the risk of parasitic glow, along with an Invar block for precise mounting and efficient thermal management. This presentation will detail the electronics and mechanical architecture, supported by thermal analysis and finite element modeling, and will present results from initial performance testing.

Items.Authors: Sebastian Remi, Sony Cheriyan, Joshua Konstantinos, Cody Hopper, Wesley Fues
Items.Title: Design and validation of a pulse tube–cooled astronomy camera for large format detectors with sub-micron sensor stability
Items.Abstract: Teledyne Digital Imaging develops highly sensitive CCD and CMOS sensors for astronomy and integrates them into complete off‑the‑shelf camera systems. As sensor size increases, however, cooling based on thermoelectric coolers can become overly complex and inefficient at achieving sufficiently low and uniform dark current performance.  Here we present recent technical developments integrating an e2v CCD‑C6 sensor into a new camera system using a Thales 9310 pulse tube cryocooler. We demonstrate a design that provides high cooling efficiency while avoiding temperature gradients with relatively low system complexity. A layered combination of passive and active vibration mitigation is used to eliminate cryocooler‑induced camera MTF degradation. The system achieves excellent sensor stability, with ≤0.5 µm displacement using the first passive layer alone. The cooling architecture is readily adaptable to other detector types, including hybrid CMOS infrared detectors.

Items.Authors: Vaishnava C. S. , Hitesh Kumar Adalja, Mithun N. P. S., Neeraj K. Tiwari, Arpit R. Patel, Bhavesh Raj Singh Nehra, B. S. Bharath Saiguhan, Shanmugam M., Santosh V. Vadawale
Items.Title: Design & development of flat-mirror X-ray concentrator optics
Items.Abstract: X-ray observations help us study some of the universe’s most extreme regions, and X-ray optics are essential for collecting photons efficiently. At PRL, we are developing a new Schmidt-based X-ray concentrator system that uses flat, orthogonally placed mirrors to focus light into a small spot suitable for a Silicon Drift Detector (SDD). This system, known as FXCO (Flat-mirror X-ray Concentrator Optics), provides a straightforward and compact approach for soft X-ray studies. One of its promising applications is pulsar-based navigation, which uses stable X-ray pulsations for spacecraft guidance. An array of FXCO modules can provide NICER-like effective area, enabling timing and spectroscopy studies. We present the design and development of a single FXCO module, along with its experimental results and simulated Crab pulse profiles as detected by this module.

Items.Authors: Xiaoxia Qiu, Chao Liu, yonghui hou, Teng Xu
Items.Title: Design of RBF-PID adaptive control strategy for nonlinear compensation in AO system
Items.Abstract: The adaptive optics (AO) system is the core technology that enhances the imaging resolution of ground-based telescopes.The control accuracy of AO systems directly determines the high-resolution observation capability of telescopes.In view of the technical bottleneck of the existing AO systems, which mostly adopt simplified control laws and fail to fully consider the time correlation of atmospheric turbulence, resulting in insufficient suppression of nonlinear disturbances and limited improvement in imaging quality,this paper aims to propose an optimized control method for AO systems that takes into account both adaptive capabilities and control accuracy.This paper designs an adaptive PID control strategy based on Radial Basis Function (RBF) neural network (RBF-PID).The core utilizes the strong nonlinear approximation capability of the RBF neural network to adaptively identify

Items.Authors: Pruchaya Sonnapapat, Supachai Awiphan, Sasikan Suriyot, Warakon Sribunrueang, Kenwit Phimprasong, Weerapot Wanajaroen, Apirat Prasit, Pongpop Sukanunta, Thansita Thomrungpiyathan, Naphat Muangnin, Natthapong Sanwongwan
Items.Title: Design of the NARIT 0.8-m Ritchey–Chrétien Telescope optical tube assembly
Items.Abstract: The National Astronomical Research Institute of Thailand (NARIT) presents the development of its first domestic telescope, a 0.8-m Ritchey–Chrétien system with a 15.6-arcminute field of view and a 309-mm back focal distance. The mechanical design and optimization of the primary mirror (M1), secondary mirror (M2), folding mirror (M3), elevation ring, and truss structure are detailed. This telescope is planned for use in public outreach activities and will also serve as a foundation for Thailand’s future telescope technology development. Finally, this paper aims to provide a basis for the design of similar telescopes.
